title: I Let Bots Into My Game Until the Server Died

answers.what: A multiplayer world that runs in the browser. Anyone with the link can walk in.
answers.how: The server sends every player's position to every other player 20 times a second, so its work grows with the square of the player count.
answers.stakes: I want real people in it. Before I invite them, I want to know where it breaks.

answers.reasoning: Outgoing bytes per second is about N x N x bytes per player x 20. Measure bytes per player from one real snapshot, then solve for the limit of the Lightsail micro.

prediction.notes: The guess stays empty until you say it on camera.

answers.built: A bot script of about 40 lines. It opens a WebSocket to staging, sends positions at the real client's rate, wanders at random, reads and discards snapshots, and logs how late each snapshot arrives against the expected 50 ms.

build.notes: Build the dashboard before filming anything: bots connected, average and worst snapshot gap, server bytes out, CPU, and a top-down view with each bot as a dot. The dashboard is most of the footage.

answers.axis: Number of bots connected at once.

runs.notes: Your laptop may choke before the server does, because every bot also receives N squared data. If it does, say so on camera and move bots to AWS. That is a run, not a failure.

twist.notes: Candidate, not confirmed: one bot that stops reading its socket. If GF-2 behaves as the audit describes, one slow connection stalls the world for everyone. Film it before planning around it.

answers.picture: N dots, each with a line to every other dot. Add dots and watch the number of lines explode.

answers.ask: Open the world and be a real player among the bots.

invite.notes: Do not promise a fix on camera. GF-2 and GF-4 are reserved as future student missions in world/gameplan.md.

rungs.change: Bots from two or three AWS regions
